transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-03 11:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Jamal (Redwood Solutions) — Lena, Devon, Aisha, Ravi (Ironwood)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on p95 and streaming token throughput. Customer leaning towards Dedicated or Private for regulatory reasons but wants to validate latency and token/sec economics first.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick intros, i'm maya -- i'm the AE on the account, connor's our SE who'll lead the benchmark stuff.
[00:12] Lena: hi, lena here. thanks, busy week, appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:16] Devon: hey all devon, platform. we'll ask a bunch about p95 and bursts.
[00:21] Aisha: aisha secops, i'll focus on compliance and encryption questions.
[00:26] Connor: great, i'll jump into technical questions and proposed benchmark plan. quick note — apologies for any audio glitches, my dog decided to join.

[00:40] Maya: high level, ironwood runs a customer chat assistant — short prompts mostly but we have long-form streaming for code and docs. p95 target is currently 350ms for short responses, but product wants to push to 200ms at p95 for premium tier. does that align with what you folks need?
[01:05] Lena: yeah, premium tier target is 200ms p95 for 16-64 token responses. For streaming long-form we want steady 60–120 tokens/sec and not drop frames. Our traffic profile has big bursts tho — black friday type spikes where concurrency jumps x10.
[01:28] Connor: ok got it. a couple of things to clarify: when you say 200ms p95 is that cold-start included? and token size distribution?
[01:36] Ravi: cold starts are rare; we mainly measure steady-state but want worst-case p95 across our fleet. average response length for short responses is 22 tokens, for streaming sessions average 800 tokens.
[01:49] Devon: we also do multi-turn with KV cache reuse, so kv-cache hit rate is around 70% on average.

[02:05] Connor: perfect. on Redwood side we measure p95 at the request/route level and can separate cold vs warm. for hosted we typically hit 150–300ms p95 for small LLMs on optimized runtimes, but for the 200ms p95 we often recommend dedicated pools with pinned exec kernels and aggressive batching control. for streaming tokens/sec — we can sustain 80–180 tokens/sec per GPU-backed stream depending on model and quantization.
[02:38] Lena: when you say per-stream, is that per-connection or per-GPU? we need a translation to threads or connections per node.
[02:45] Connor: per-stream meaning a single streaming response. on hardware it's constrained by model decode throughput; multiple streams multiplex on the same GPU with continuous batching. we can give more precise tokens/sec numbers once we know model (e.g., Llama 2 13B vs 70B).

[03:05] Maya: quick hosting tradeoff — hosted is fastest to onboard, dedicated gives predictability and reserved throughput, private gives you VPC and KMS control for compliance. most customers doing p95 <250ms at scale choose dedicated or private.
[03:20] Aisha: compliance is key. we need KMS with HSM-backed keys, audit logs with retention 7 years, SAML SSO, and per-token retention controls. do you support that in private?
[03:35] Jamal: yes, private can include customer-managed KMS, audit log streaming to your logging endpoint, and we support SAML/SSO/RBAC. we'll share the security pack.

[03:48] Devon: ok on benchmarks — what's the process and how long? we want to run realistic traffic, include KV cache behavior, varied token lengths, and bursts.
[03:59] Connor: recommended path: you provide a redacted traffic CSV with per-route token length distribution, concurrency curves, and KV-hit estimates. we run a 48-hour continuous benchmark on representative model(s) and hosting modes to capture steady-state and burst behavior. output: p95 latency numbers, tokens/sec sustained per model, cost/sec and failure scenarios.
[04:20] Lena: we'd like to run experiments with quantization as well — 4-bit/8-bit tradeoffs. any surprises there?
[04:27] Connor: quantization usually reduces memory and cost, but can add decode variance. for some models 4-bit quantization shows a slight increase in p95 jitter. we capture that in the benchmark and also recommend rollbacks to higher-precision variants for premium routes.

[04:45] Ravi: does Redwood do automatic fallback for capacity—like route to smaller model when large ones are busy?
[04:50] Maya: yes, smart routing policy — we can configure route-based fallbacks, region failover, and capacity tiers. for SLAs we typically suggest canary fallback windows.

[05:05] Devon: the burst scenario — assume baseline concurrency 150 and burst to 1,500 for 10 minutes. what happens with hosted vs dedicated?
[05:15] Connor: hosted can absorb short bursts with elastic capacity but may have cold-start tails; dedicated is pre-reserved so p95 is far more stable during burst if you size correctly or provide burst credits. private you'd size and autoscale within your infra. for that magnitude of burst we recommend a hybrid: dedicated baseline + small hosted fallback for overspill.

[05:46] Aisha: security question — can we keep logs off Redwood for PII routes? we need tokens never persisted for certain routes.
[05:54] Jamal: yes, route-level retention controls — redact or disable logs per route, and private deployment can be configured to avoid storing any request content in Redwood-managed storage.

[06:08] Lena: ok good. any limitations on tokens/sec for streaming at very large scale? we plan for 10k concurrent streaming sessions at peak in one region — is that realistic?
[06:18] Connor: 10k concurrent streams is large but achievable with cluster sizing across GPUs and smart batching. key is avg tokens/sec per stream — at 80 tokens/sec it'd be very heavy. we'd run benchmarks with a scaled prototype for that. cost also grows linearly with token throughput.

[06:35] Devon: can you show an example deliverable from a benchmark?
[06:38] Connor: sure — example rows: model, quant, p50,p95,p99 latency, sustained tokens/sec, concurrency per GPU, cost per 1M tokens, error rate under burst. we'll upload a template.

[06:55] Lena: timeline — we want results within a week. is that feasible?
[06:58] Maya: feasible for the initial 48-hour run plus preliminary analysis — we'll aim to deliver a results deck by Apr 8.

[07:05] Ravi: one more — network egress and region placement matter. we need EU-only for some customers. can you pin a region?
[07:12] Jamal: yes, region pinning supported in dedicated/private and hosted with regional endpoints. we'll note EU compliance in the security pack.

[07:25] Aisha: SSO and audit log retention — please include sample retention policy and a schema of audit events.
[07:31] Maya: will do.

[07:36] Devon: question around multiplexed connections — how do you measure per-connection latency when batching is happening?
[07:42] Connor: we instrument at the route ingress and egress and include KV-cache hit tags; we can break out observed queueing time, kernel time, and decode time so you can see batching contribution to p95. sometimes p95 is driven by long decode rather than queueing.

[08:05] Lena: any gotchas we should know before we start the benchmark?
[08:08] Connor: ensure redacted but realistic payloads; include header patterns that matter (like cookie/session sizes); and note that for streaming, we need to run the client-side behavior (ack windows) to simulate real tokens/sec, not just firehose.

[08:28] Maya: ok let's capture next steps: we'll run the 48-hour benchmark and share results, security pack, and a pricing/pilot proposal after results.
[08:37] Lena: sounds good. thanks.

[08:40] Connor: i'll own the benchmark and post the spreadsheet.
[08:43] Aisha: and i'll put together the compliance checklist from our side.

[08:47] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the scoping call.

[08:51] Devon: great, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes (auto): transcription had occasional word swaps ("K-V cash" for KV cache, "quantizaton"), timestamps approximate. Customer emphasized 200ms p95 for short responses and 60–120 tokens/sec streaming target; large bursts up to x10 concurrency observed; they require HSM/KMS and long-term audit logs.
